episodes.title: What’s Driving Elon Musk?
episodes.description:
Ahead of the midterm elections, Elon Musk has become the single largest campaign donor in any election cycle, giving about $450 million to Republicans. It is just a fraction of a percent of his near-trillion-dollar net worth.
Musk’s control over SpaceX, Starlink, X, Tesla and Neuralink, on top of his riches, has given him power over wealth, attention and critical infrastructure that few human beings have ever amassed before. What does he want to do with all this power? What is he trying to buy with his campaign spending? What is the world he wants to build?
Quinn Slobodian is a professor of international history at Boston University. He’s the author of “Globalists,” “Hayek’s Bastards” and, most recently, “Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed,” which he co-wrote with Ben Tarnoff.

episodes.title: Can Elon Musk Buy His Way Out of a Reckoning?
episodes.description:
With less than a week to go until Election Day, Elon Musk is once again at the center of American politics. The world's richest man has poured nearly half a billion dollars into the midterms to stave off Democratic gains. Meanwhile, Republican and Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation following revelations that Musk restricted Ukraine’s access to Starlink. And last week, Musk threatened Kara with jail time on X after she said he could face investigations if Democrats return to power. 



Kara brings together a panel of experts to unpack the business interests behind Musk’s political bets: why he's spending big on the Texas Senate race, what’s driving a potential Tesla–SpaceX merger and whether a post-election reckoning could bring accountability and check his power. 



Kirsten Grind is an investigative business reporter at The New York Times covering Silicon Valley and tech executives, including Elon Musk. Catherine Rampell is the Economics Editor for The Bulwark and an MSNOW contributor. Faiz Siddiqui is a tech reporter at The Washington Post and author of the book Hubris Maximus: The Shattering of Elon Musk.

Elon Musk has spent his career turning improbable ideas into companies that reshape the world. To some, the entrepreneur behind Tesla and SpaceX is an engineering genius whose ambitions have transformed electric cars and space travel. To others, his politics and extraordinary influence raise serious questions about the future he is building. A candid conversation about the imagination, drive and contradictions of a man determined to turn his vision into our future.

E1197: Elon Musk's Grokipedia went from 6.5 million monthly Google clicks in July to just 200,000. That's a 97% collapse in organic search traffic for xAI's entirely AI-written alternative to Wikipedia.
 And despite Grokipedia earning backlinks from The New York Times, The Guardian, NPR, NBC News, The Verge, and other major publications, its rankings have fallen off a cliff.
 I break down what happened to Grokipedia, the Google policies its AI content runs into, and the lessons every SEO needs to understand before scaling AI-generated content.
 Here's what I cover:
 1. Grokipedia's 97% SEO traffic collapse
 - How Grokipedia reached 5.8 million monthly Google clicks by January 2026.
 - Why traffic fell to 1.5 million in May, recovered to 6.5 million in July, and then collapsed to 200,000.
 - Why major media coverage, powerful backlinks, and Elon Musk's influence haven't protected its Google rankings.
 - Why early traffic growth doesn't guarantee long-term SEO success.
 2. The Google policies Grokipedia runs into
 - Google's scaled content abuse policy and its rules against mass-producing unoriginal content.
 - Google's scraping policy and its restrictions on republishing existing information without substantial added value.
 - Why Grokipedia's fully automated approach raises concerns under both policies.
 - Google's October 1 AI content guideline changes and its explicit instructions to manually fact-check and review AI-generated content before publishing.
 - Why using AI to fact-check AI doesn't satisfy the human-review standard Google describes.
 3. Other explanations for Grokipedia's collapse
 - Why users might trust human-edited Wikipedia more than an entirely AI-generated encyclopedia.
 - How poor user signals and declining trust might contribute to falling rankings.
 - How Google's AI Overviews compete directly with informational websites.
 - Why Wikipedia itself has suffered a major decline in organic search traffic.
 - Why we can't conclude that Google issued Grokipedia a penalty.
 4. What Grokipedia's backlinks reveal
 - Why most of Grokipedia's major press backlinks point to its homepage.
 - How Wikipedia benefits from links pointing directly to its individual articles.
 - Why building links to subpages, category pages, and content hubs matters.
 - How site structure and internal linking distribute authority throughout a website.
 5. Lessons for SEOs using AI content
 - Why you need to manually review AI-generated articles, landing pages, and metadata before publishing.
 - Why one-shot AI content often misses important aspects of search intent.
 - How to use noindex until your AI content passes human review.
 - Why you shouldn't mistake the initial traffic surge from scaled AI content for lasting success.
 - Why I recommend keeping aggressive AI experiments separate from valuable, established websites.
 - What Google says about recovery times after fixing serious SEO problems.
 I also discuss three possible futures for Grokipedia: continued decline, Elon Musk publicly challenging Google, or xAI finding another purpose for its AI-generated encyclopedia.
 The bigger lesson: If you're building a website for long-term organic traffic, don't sacrifice content quality and human oversight just to publish more pages.

episodes.title: From Fair Game: Sam Altman Talks Elon Musk, ‘Artificial,’ and the Future of Humanity (Part 1 of 2)
episodes.description:
Every day a new scientific breakthrough or existential threat seems to make the world more aware and more distrusting of an AI future that we’re told is rapidly approaching—whether we like it or not. And nobody is more recognized as the face of artificial intelligence—as a technology, an industry, and a civilizational shift—than Open AI founder and CEO Sam Altman. Long before he became a household name, Altman established a towering reputation in Silicon Valley: persuasive prodigy, visionary futurist, relentless CEO. But as OpenAI’s influence broke out of tech’s insular bubble, some of the very same traits that served him well in Northern California have become his greatest liabilities. In a far-ranging conversation taped in San Francisco on September 11th – the first of two sitdowns with Vanity Fair’s Mark Guiducci –  Altman discusses his views on ChatGPT and suicide prevention, safety breaches, and the film ‘Artificial,’ in which Andrew Garfield plays him—along with much more.  “I understand the instinct to say, ‘I don't want the change, I don't want the risk. Just stop it,’” Altman says. “I really hope that hundreds of years from now people look back at our lives and just can't believe how bad we had it.”



This is the first installment of a two-part interview with Altman. You can find the second installment on YouTube and podcast apps now.

episodes.description:
For a decade, Elon Musk was the face of the modern entrepreneur: a self-made billionaire who bet his fortune on impossible ideas and somehow made them work.
SpaceX made reusable rockets a reality. Tesla helped turn electric cars into a global phenomenon. He became one of the most admired and influential figures in technology.
So what happened?
In this episode of In the Blink of AI, Georgie Healy traces Musk’s journey from bullied South African kid and PayPal millionaire to the man behind Tesla, SpaceX, Starlink, X, xAI and more. Along the way, we explore the moments that transformed his public image: the Tesla “funding secured” controversy, his increasingly combative behavior online, his influence over Starlink during the war in Ukraine, his takeover of Twitter, his political rise alongside Donald Trump, and the controversies surrounding Grok.
But this isn’t simply a takedown.
Using the 4Gs framework, Georgie asks the harder question: Was Elon Musk actually a genius, or was he simply in the right place at the right time?
The answer is more complicated than either side might want to admit.
Because Musk may genuinely have helped solve some of the hardest engineering problems of our time. But does extraordinary capability excuse harmful behaviour?
You be the judge.

This week: SpaceX reports its first quarter as a public company, and Elon Musk says Starlink could deliver a majority of the world's internet within a decade, leveraging production facilities in Redmond. More To The Story: Boston University professor Quinn Slobodian discusses his book “Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed,” which he co-authored with Ben Tarnoff. They outline how Elon Musk’s background and political views have reshaped capitalism and coin new terms to describe the unique ways Musk has been able to forge a close and symbiotic relationship with the government. On this week’s More To The Story, host Al Letson talks with Slobodian about how the world’s richest person has reimagined the relationship between business and government, his unique brand of futurism, and how Musk’s early life in apartheid South Africa ultimately shaped his worldview.
